implementation_notes: No standard or dominant C++ persistence library hands you a session identity map, so the classic structure is hand-written: a session/unit-of-work object owns a std::unordered_map keyed on the identity (type plus primary key) and exposes find_or_load, returning the stored shared_ptr on a hit and inserting on a miss; weak_ptr is the alternative when the map must not extend object lifetimes. The classic form stays justified because the C++ standard library has no persistence context; when you do use an ORM that provides a session-level cache, prefer that context and do not stack a second map on top.
pitfalls: Rehashing invalidates iterators (but not references or pointers) of std::unordered_map: never hold iterators across inserts - hold a reference or shared_ptr instead.
shared_ptr cycles: an entity owning a shared_ptr back to the session that owns it keeps the whole session alive; back-references should be weak_ptr.
std::unordered_map is not thread-safe; a session is thread-confined or must be synchronised externally.
